summary: Void Voyagers is an offline health monitor that helps astronauts check, understand and act on their own health. On a Mars mission a message to Earth can take up to 22 minutes each way, so the crew must spot problems itself. Astronauts log 15 guided self-checks, such as heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2, temperature, blood glucose, sleep, mood and a reaction-time test. Each reading is checked against NASA-STD-3001 limits and clinical ranges and shown in colour, shape and words (Nominal, Watch, Act or Urgent), with one next step worded for the signal delay. A clickable 3D anatomy body shows every system's function and status, trend charts and routine streaks keep the habit going, and a library of 61 conditions and 58 medicines explains risks and label doses. Emergency and solar-storm tools, a Mind companion for isolation and an offline report for flight surgeons complete it. It works with no internet and keeps health data on the device. The same private checks could help polar crews, sailors and remote communities on Earth.
details:
Void Voyagers: stay well beyond Earth. An offline health monitor that helps astronauts check, understand and act on their own health.

THE PROBLEM

Long missions expose astronauts to NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile closed environments. They can bring bone and muscle loss, fluid shifts and vision changes, immune changes, cardiovascular events and behavioural health problems. On the space station a flight surgeon is a call away; on a Mars mission a message can take up to 22 minutes each way. The crew has to spot health changes and act on them itself.

OUR SOLUTION: CHECK, UNDERSTAND, ACT

  • Check: 15 guided self-checks, including resting heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2, body temperature, blood glucose, sleep, mood, a PHQ-4 wellbeing check, a reaction-time test, a near-vision and Amsler grid check, fluids, exercise, radiation dose, cabin CO2 and body mass. Each has step-by-step instructions and explains why it matters in space.
  • Understand: every reading gets a colour, a shape and a word (Nominal, Watch, Act or Urgent), based on NASA-STD-3001 limits and clinical ranges, with the reason shown.
  • Act: one clear next step, worded for the mission’s signal delay, including when to tell the crew medical officer and when to contact flight surgeons on the ground.

HOW IT WORKS

  • Mission environments: LEO station, Moon base, Mars transit and Mars base, with the signal delay to Earth worked out from JPL planetary positions.
  • Daily routine: the console lists each check with its schedule, tracks what is done today, and rewards the routine with streaks, levels and badges.
  • 3D body map: a clickable anatomy model built from BodyParts3D, with muscle, organ, bone and status views for male and female bodies. Tapping a system shows what it does, what spaceflight does to it, its checks and its status.
  • Trends: charts of every indicator over 7, 14 or 30 days.
  • Library: 61 conditions and 58 medicines in plain language, backed by 527 source links. Medicines show their label dose; for medicines where it is safe, the dose is worked out from the astronaut’s own vital signs and never goes above the label maximum.
  • Mind: a daily check-in companion for isolation, clocks and countdowns for home, short guided exercises, and a private journal and letters space encrypted with a passphrase.
  • Deep-space tools: an emergency log, an “I feel unwell” symptom guide, solar-storm shelter steps with live NASA DONKI space-weather alerts, and a medicine-kit expiry tracker.
  • Reports: a flight-surgeon report the astronaut reads before sending, a short text code that can be read out over a weak link, and an outbox that sends reports when the connection returns.

ANSWERING THE CHALLENGE

  • Which measurements can be done in space? Only checks a crew can do with onboard equipment, each with how-to steps.
  • Why is an exam needed, and how do hazards affect it? Every check and body system explains this in plain words.
  • When does a result need the crew or flight surgeons? The verdict says so directly, adjusted to the signal delay.
  • What actions prevent a critical condition? Each finding gives the next step and links to the library.
  • Potential considerations: different environments, routine prompts, gamification, dynamic charts, colour coding and simple instructions are all built in.

TECHNICAL IMPLEMENTATION

  • One HTML, CSS and JavaScript web app with no framework. A service worker makes it work fully offline and installable like an app.
  • Health data stays on the device (browser storage with a second IndexedDB copy), with backup, import and SQL export.
  • The 3D body uses BodyParts3D meshes processed in Python (trimesh, fast-simplification, scikit-image), compressed with gltfpack and rendered with three.js.
  • Reports go to an insert-only Supabase inbox with row-level security, a rate limit and automatic deletion after 90 days.
  • Security and quality: a strict Content Security Policy, AES-GCM encryption with PBKDF2 (600,000 iterations) for the private space, two penetration tests, a built-in self-test and automated browser tests.
  • Hosted at voidvoyagers.earth on Vercel, with an Azure Static Web Apps mirror. Open source on GitHub under the MIT licence.

CREATIVITY AND IMPACT

Instead of a wall of numbers, Void Voyagers gives one verdict and one next step, adapts its advice to the signal delay, and treats mental health as part of health. It is private by design: no accounts, no cookies, and data stays on the device. On Earth, the same offline checks could help polar and Antarctic crews, sailors, analogue missions and remote communities far from a clinic.

HOW WE USED AI

We used Claude (Anthropic) to research and summarise NASA and medical sources, check facts, write and debug code, test security, and draft text and the slide design. The team reviewed the medical content and its sources. No AI runs inside the app, and the app uses no AI-generated images.

LIMITATIONS

Void Voyagers is a research and training prototype, not a medical device. Readings are entered by hand; it does not connect to sensors. It supports, and does not replace, the crew medical officer and flight surgeons.

TEAM

Temuulen Buuveibaatar (lead developer), Ulugbek Yuldashov (co-developer, front end, research and testing), Orkhon Munkh-Oron (co-developer and testing), Erdenebaatar Ankhzaya (researcher) and Bat-Erdene Munkhkhuslen (designer).
